nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are the nutrient sources mentioned for organic farming?
nodes.answer: Nutrient sources in organic farming include agricultural waste, animal manure produced on the farm, and biological nitrogen fixation.
nodes.paragraph: Various species can be used, and mixtures of species can provide a variety of ser - vices (Justes 2017). Legumes can be used to increase the nitrogen (N) input to the soil through biological N fixation from the atmosphere (Tribouillois et al. 2016; Herridge et al. 2008). Cover crops, including legumes, are important especially in organic farm- ing systems, where they contribute with a significant share of the input of N to the main crops (Berry et al. 2006). In organic farming, synthetic chemicals are not allowed, including fertilizers, herbicides and pes- ticides (EC 2023; Hansen et al. 2001). Protection of ecological, human, and animal health are key motiva- tors for the expansion of organic farming in Denmark, which is the country with the highest market share of organic food in the world (EU CAP Network 2023). In organic farming, nutrient sources include agricul- tural waste and animal manure produced on the farm, and biological N fixation (Watson et al. 2006).

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: When were the applications of manure and straw performed?
nodes.answer: The applications of manure and straw were performed following the crop harvest in the Autumn.
nodes.paragraph: Cow dung was applied at the rate of 5130 kg ha 1 per year as manure fertilizer. The previous sea- son S crop straw was used for the straw application. Detailed nitrogen, phosphorous, and potassium nutrient inputs for each treatment are provided in Table S1. Application of manure and straw were performed follow - ing the crop harvest in the Autumn. Diammonium phos- phate and potassium sulphate, along with 50% of the N fertilizer (the N shortage was replenished by urea), were applied before sowing in the Spring. The remaining N fer - tilizer as urea was applied at the bolting stage. A popular sorghum cultivar, Jinza 31, was seeded with a plant den- sity of 120,0 plant ha 1 in April 2020, and harvested in September 2020. The growing season experienced no obvi- ous issues with pests, diseases, or weed infestations. Soils attached to the surface of five sorghum plant roots were col - lected at the jointing, heading, filling and maturity stages in 2020 as rhizosphere soils. The rhizosphere soil samples were immediately taken to the laboratory and sieved soils to < 2 mm, and stored at 80 C for molecular analyses.
